*Purpose*: We've been learning how to quantify uncertainty in estimates through the exercises; now its time to put those skills to use studying real data. In this challenge we'll use concepts like confidence intervals to help us make sense of census data.

*Reading*:
- [Using ACS Estimates and Margin of Error](https://www.census.gov/data/academy/webinars/2020/calculating-margins-of-error-acs.html) (Optional, see the PDF on the page)
- [Patterns and Causes of Uncertainty in the American Community Survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0143622813002518?casa_token=VddzQ1-spHMAAAAA:FTq92LXgiPVloJUVjnHs8Ma1HwvPigisAYtzfqaGbbRRwoknNq56Y2IzszmGgIGH4JAPzQN0) (Optional, particularly the *Uncertainty in surveys* section under the Introduction.)

# Setup
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
```

### __q1__ Load the population data from c06; simply replace `filename_pop` below.

```{r q1-task}
## TODO: Give the filename for your copy of Table B01003
filename_pop <- "./data/ACSDT5Y2018.B01003-Data.csv"

## NOTE: No need to edit
df_pop <-
  read_csv(
    filename_pop,
    skip = 1,
  ) %>% 
  rename(
    population_estimate = `Estimate!!Total`
  )

df_pop
```

You might wonder why the `Margin of Error` in the population estimates is listed as `*****`. From the [documentation (PDF link)](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwj81Omy16TrAhXsguAKHTzKDQEQFjABegQIBxAB&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww2.census.gov%2Fprograms-surveys%2Facs%2Ftech_docs%2Faccuracy%2FMultiyearACSAccuracyofData2018.pdf%3F&usg=AOvVaw2TOrVuBDlkDI2gde6ugce_) for the ACS:

> If the margin of error is displayed as ‘*****’ (five asterisks), the estimate has been controlled to be equal to a fixed value and so it has no sampling error. A standard error of zero should be used for these controlled estimates when completing calculations, such as those in the following section.

This means that for cases listed as `*****` the US Census Bureau recommends treating the margin of error (and thus standard error) as zero.

### __q2__ Obtain median income data from the Census Bureau:

- `Filter > Topics > Income and Poverty > Income and Poverty`
- `Filter > Geography > County > All counties in United States`
- Look for `Median Income in the Past 12 Months` (Table S1903)
- Download the 2018 5-year ACS estimates; save to your `data` folder and add the filename below.

```{r q2-task}
## TODO: Give the filename for your copy of Table S1903
filename_income <- "./data/ACSST5Y2018.S1903-Data.csv"

## NOTE: No need to edit
df_income <-
  read_csv(filename_income, skip = 1)
df_income
```

Use the following test to check that you downloaded the correct file:

```{r q2-tests}
## NOTE: No need to edit, use to check you got the right file.
assertthat::assert_that(
  df_income %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001") %>%
    pull(`Estimate!!Percent Distribution!!FAMILY INCOME BY FAMILY SIZE!!2-person families`)
  == 45.6
)

print("Well done!")
```


This dataset is in desperate need of some *tidying*. To simplify the task, we'll start by considering the `\\d-person families` columns first.

### __q3__ Tidy the `df_income` dataset by completing the code below. Pivot and rename the columns to arrive at the column names `id, geographic_area_name, category, income_estimate, income_moe`.

*Hint*: You can do this in a single pivot using the `".value"` argument and a `names_pattern` using capture groups `"()"`. Remember that you can use an OR operator `|` in a regex to allow for multiple possibilities in a capture group, for example `"(Estimate|Margin of Error)"`.

```{r q3-task}
df_q3 <-
  df_income %>%
  select(
    Geography,
    contains("Geographic"),
    # This will select only the numeric d-person family columns;
    # it will ignore the annotation columns
    contains("median") & matches("\\d-person families") & !contains("Annotation of")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(contains("median"), as.numeric)) %>%
  # one row per county and family size with the estimate and moe as columns
  pivot_longer(
    names_to = c(".value", "category"),
    names_pattern = "(Estimate|Margin of Error)!!.*!!(\\d-person families)",
    cols = c(-Geography, -`Geographic Area Name`)
  ) %>%
  rename(
    geographic_area_name = `Geographic Area Name`,
    income_estimate = Estimate,
    income_moe = `Margin of Error`
  )

df_q3 %>%
  glimpse()
```

Use the following tests to check your work:

```{r q3-tests}
## NOTE: No need to edit
assertthat::assert_that(setequal(
  names(df_q3),
  c("Geography", "geographic_area_name", "category", "income_estimate", "income_moe")
))

assertthat::assert_that(
  df_q3 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_moe)
  == 6663
)

print("Nice!")
```


The data gives finite values for the Margin of Error, which is closely related to the Standard Error. The Census Bureau documentation gives the following relationship between Margin of Error and Standard Error:

$$\text{MOE} = 1.645 \times \text{SE}.$$

### __q4__ Convert the margin of error to standard error. Additionally, compute a 99% confidence interval on income, and normalize the standard error to `income_CV = income_SE / income_estimate`. Provide these columns with the names `income_SE, income_lo, income_hi, income_CV`.

```{r q4-task}
# moe is 1.645 standard errors and a 99% interval uses the 0.995 quantile
df_q4 <-
  df_q3 %>%
  mutate(
    income_SE = income_moe / 1.645,
    income_lo = income_estimate - qnorm(1 - (1 - 0.99) / 2) * income_SE,
    income_hi = income_estimate + qnorm(1 - (1 - 0.99) / 2) * income_SE,
    income_CV = income_SE / income_estimate
  )

df_q4
```

Use the following tests to check your work:

```{r q4-tests}
## NOTE: No need to edit
assertthat::assert_that(setequal(
  names(df_q4),
  c("Geography", "geographic_area_name", "category", "income_estimate", "income_moe",
    "income_SE", "income_lo", "income_hi", "income_CV")
))

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_SE) - 4050.456
  ) / 4050.456 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_lo) - 54513.72
  ) / 54513.72 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_hi) - 75380.28
  ) / 75380.28 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_CV) - 0.06236556
  ) / 0.06236556 < 1e-3
)

print("Nice!")
```


One last wrangling step: We need to join the two datasets so we can compare population with income.

### __q5__ Join `df_q4` and `df_pop`.

```{r q5-task}
## TODO: Join df_q4 and df_pop by the appropriate column
df_data <-
  df_q4 %>%
  left_join(df_pop, by = "Geography")

df_data
```

# Analysis
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

We now have both estimates and confidence intervals for `\\d-person families`. Now we can compare cases with quantified uncertainties: Let's practice!

### __q6__ Study the following graph, making sure to note what you can *and can't* conclude based on the estimates and confidence intervals. Document your observations below and answer the questions.

```{r q6-task}
## NOTE: No need to edit; run and inspect
wid <- 0.5

df_data %>%
  filter(str_detect(geographic_area_name, "Massachusetts")) %>%
  mutate(
    county = str_remove(geographic_area_name, " County,.*$"),
    county = fct_reorder(county, income_estimate)
  ) %>%

  ggplot(aes(county, income_estimate, color = category)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = income_lo, ymax = income_hi),
    position = position_dodge(width = wid)
  ) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = wid)) +

  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "County",
    y = "Median Household Income"
  )
```

```{r q6-population}
# population of each massachusetts county, smallest first
df_pop %>%
  filter(str_detect(`Geographic Area Name`, "Massachusetts")) %>%
  select(`Geographic Area Name`, population_estimate) %>%
  arrange(population_estimate)
```

**Observations**:

- Document your observations here.
  - The counties are sorted by income, with Norfolk at the top and Suffolk at the bottom of the plot.
  - In every county except Nantucket, the red 2-person point is the farthest left. Two-person families have the lowest median income in almost every county.
  - The red 2-person intervals are short in most counties, while the pink 6-person intervals are usually the longest. The intervals tend to get wider as family size goes up, which fits with there being fewer large families to survey.
  - Dukes and Nantucket have no 6-person point. The Census did not report a 6-person estimate for them, which is why the plot warns that 2 rows were removed.
  - The y axis label says household income. These values are actually median family income for each family size.
- Can you confidently distinguish between household incomes in Suffolk county? Why or why not?
  - No. All five Suffolk intervals overlap each other just below the 75000 gridline. The points go up from 2-person to 6-person families. The intervals are wide enough that the true medians could be in a different order. I can't say with 99% confidence that any family size in Suffolk has a higher median income than another.
- Which counties have the widest confidence intervals?
  - Nantucket and Dukes. The blue 5-person interval for Nantucket stretches from near 0 to past the 200000 gridline. Dukes has the next widest intervals. The population table shows these are the two smallest counties in Massachusetts, with 11101 and 17313 people. Fewer people means fewer families in the survey, which makes the estimates less certain.

In the next task you'll investigate the relationship between population and uncertainty.

### __q7__ Plot the standard error against population for all counties. Create a visual that effectively highlights the trends in the data. Answer the questions under *observations* below.

*Hint*: Remember that standard error is a function of *both* variability (e.g. variance) and sample size.

```{r q7-task, message = FALSE}
# one panel per family size so the trend is not mixed across sizes
df_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(income_SE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(population_estimate, income_SE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(color = "red") +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~category) +
  labs(
    x = "County population (log scale)",
    y = "Standard error of median income (dollars, log scale)"
  )
```

**Observations**:

- What *overall* trend do you see between `SE` and population? Why might this trend exist?
  - The standard error goes down as population goes up. In every panel, the points slope down from left to right and the red trend line goes down. In the 2-person panel, the trend line starts above the 10K gridline for the smallest counties and ends below the 1K gridline at 10M people.
  - The ACS surveys a sample of households in each county. A county with more people has more families in the sample. The standard error shrinks as the sample size grows, just like SE = sigma / sqrt(n) shrinks as n gets bigger.
  - The points also spread out a lot up and down at any one population. Standard error depends on how spread out incomes are in a county and not only on sample size.
  - The cloud of points is higher in the 6-person panel than in the 2-person panel. The 6-person trend line stays near or above the 10K gridline until about 100K people, while the 2-person line drops below 10K by about 1K people. There are fewer 6-person families in each county, which gives a smaller sample for that group.
- What does this *overall* trend tell you about the relative ease of studying small vs large counties?
  - Large counties are much easier to study. Their estimates have small standard errors and narrow intervals. Small counties have large standard errors, like Nantucket and Dukes in q6. To get a precise estimate for a small county I would need more data for that county, such as combining more years of the survey or surveying a larger share of its households.

# Going Further
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

Now it's your turn! You have income data for every county in the United States: Pose your own question and try to answer it with the data.

### __q8__ Pose your own question about the data. Create a visualization (or table) here, and document your observations.

**Question**: Does median family income keep going up as families get bigger and how sure can we be for the larger family sizes?

```{r q8-task}
## TODO: Pose and answer your own question about the data
# counties with an estimate, typical income, and typical cv for each size
df_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(income_estimate)) %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarize(
    counties = n(),
    median_income = median(income_estimate),
    median_CV = median(income_CV)
  )

df_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(income_estimate)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(category, income_estimate)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Family size",
    y = "Median family income (dollars)"
  )
```

**Observations**:

- Median income goes up from 2-person to 4-person families and then levels off. In the table, the median across counties is 56659 for 2-person families, 64133 for 3-person families, and 73627 for 4-person families. It is 71908 for 5-person families and 72236 for 6-person families, which is close to the 4-person value.
- The boxplot also shows this. The boxes for 4-person, 5-person, and 6-person families are at similar heights. The 2-person box is the lowest and the narrowest.
- The larger family sizes are less certain. The median CV goes up from 0.0487 for 2-person families to 0.173 for 6-person families. Fewer counties have an estimate at all, with 3219 counties for 2-person families and only 2653 for 6-person families.
- This means the levelling off after 4-person families is not conclusive. The differences between 4-person, 5-person, and 6-person families are under 2000 dollars, while a typical 6-person estimate has a standard error of about 17% of the estimate. Each county also counts equally here no matter how many people live there.
- To check whether income really levels off, I would need the same table for the whole United States instead of for each county. A national estimate would be based on many more families and have a much smaller margin of error for each family size.

Ideas:

- Compare trends across counties that are relevant to you; e.g. places you've lived, places you've been, places in the US that are interesting to you.
- In q3 we tidied the median `\\d-person families` columns only.
  - Tidy the other median columns to learn about other people groups.
  - Tidy the percentage columns to learn about how many households of each category are in each county.
- Your own idea!
